name: Fortify on death
summary: The first blow that would destroy the vehicle does not. The hull drops where it is as a fortified shell with fresh health and a fortification's armour, and never moves again. Riders lose a large share of their health in the crash (half their full health in the game's code, so riders already at half or less die, though the wiki says all survive at half health); the rest fight on from inside. The shell stands until destroyed, which in the source kills whoever is still inside; once the last rider climbs out, it falls apart. It happens once per life. Timed versions sit helpless in the shell for a few seconds and come back if it survives, whole or with the health it has left. Levers: the shell's health, what still works from it, who survives its fall, and whether it can be entered by choice.
counterplay: Plan for two kills: the fresh bar is the second half of the job, so keep shooting after the crash.
Change weapons: the shell is armoured like a fortification, so bring what breaks buildings, and since it can't move, shell it from beyond its riders' reach.
Choose where it dies: the shell stands wherever the hull was killed, so finish the vehicle in the open or away from the objective, then walk around it.
Deal with the riders: they are already hurt by the crash, and a shell with nobody inside falls apart, so anything that kills or drives out riders ends the second life early.
Hit the heap: when the shell goes, whoever comes out is hurt and bunched together, which is what splash is for.
Against the timed versions, destroy the shell before its timer runs out, while the unit inside can't act.

other_examples.note: An unarmed carrier for two infantry squads that turns into a fixed bunker either on the player's order or by itself the first time it would be destroyed, and can never pack up again. As a bunker it gains health on top of what it had, takes far less damage, makes room for a third squad and lets its squads fire out, which they could not do while it drove. Only repair drones can mend it. The wiki says the squads inside die with the bunker, and calls the unit almost the same as the Battle Bus. EA's unit file sets the deployment up as a 'second chance' that comes with a heal, but in that file the riders are not killed when the unit dies (its KillPassengersOnDeath setting is off), so the two sources disagree on who survives the bunker's fall.

sources.title: NODBunkerTruck.xml, Kane's Wrath unit data in Electronic Arts' CnC_Modding_Support repository on GitHub
sources.note: The publisher's own release of the game's unit files. Read for the second-chance deployment with its heal, the extra passenger slot once deployed, the riders being allowed to attack only once deployed, and the transport setting that does not kill the riders when the unit dies.

other_examples.note: The timed version on a flyer that the Blood Mage creates with his ultimate spell: when the Phoenix dies it turns into an egg with a small health pool. If the enemy fails to destroy the egg within a short time, the Phoenix hatches again; if they break it, it is gone.

sources.title: Phoenix, Warcraft III unit pages on Blizzard's Classic Battle.net site

shooter_analogues.note: A player-controlled version of the timed shell: when a blow would kill her, and the passive is not on its long cooldown, she becomes an egg for a few seconds with her health refilled. She can't act while in it, and her resistances are lower than usual early in the match and higher late. If the egg lives through the timer she returns with whatever health it has left.

sources.title: Template:Data Anivia/I (Rebirth), League of Legends Wiki

shooter_analogues.note: For contrast, a second bar that does not park the unit: a Titan whose health and shields are gone carries on in a burning state with a striped bar that normally can't be repaired, and any enemy finisher ends it at once. In the first game the bar drains by itself, so the pilot has to get out; in the second it holds, but pulling the Titan's battery or dropping a grenade into it kills it outright. This sits nearer the critical-burn armour model than this pattern.

player_translation.summary: You drive a carrier full of teammates. When its health runs out it does not blow up: it crashes down as a parked bunker with a fresh, tougher health bar. Everyone inside is hurt by the crash but stays in and keeps firing from the ports. When the shell is finally destroyed, everyone is thrown out hurt. Anyone may climb out early, and once the shell is empty it crumbles.
as_user: As the driver, where you die becomes a choice: when the hull is nearly gone you steer for the spot where a bunker helps most, such as the objective or a choke point.
After the crash you can't drive, so your seat turns into one more firing port and you fight with your sidearm beside your riders.
As a rider you lose a chunk of health in the crash and keep a protected firing position; you decide whether to hold it or to break out.
The shell is a last stand: it buys time for teammates to arrive or for an engineer to patch it, not a way back to a working vehicle.
It happens once per life; when the shell is gone you buy a new unit.
as_target: You see the hull flung up and slammed down, its outline change and a new bar with a bunker icon appear: the kill is not finished.
It can't move, so you can back out of its riders' reach, come at its blind side, bring a weapon that breaks fortifications, or leave it and take ground elsewhere.
The players inside are already hurt, and they come out hurt again when it falls.
Part of the reward is paid at the crash and the rest when the shell falls, so the first half of the work is not wasted.
teammates: Riders make the shell dangerous: its firepower is whoever stayed inside, so a full carrier leaves a strong bunker and an empty one leaves almost nothing.
The team gets a forward strongpoint where the carrier died: medics treat the hurt riders, an engineer repairs the shell, and others fight around it.
The enemy team needs to call the second bar out, bring a player with a fortification-breaking weapon, and keep a splash weapon ready for the moment it falls.
controls: The base pattern is triggered and spends no counted key: it happens by itself on the blow that would destroy the vehicle.
Inside the shell everyone aims and fires from a port as before: the mouse aims, left mouse fires.
E leaves the shell and hold X bails out; when the last player leaves, the shell crumbles after a moment, and nobody can get back in.
The anchor-by-choice twist adds a counted key: hold Q to drop into the shell on purpose, one way.
feedback: The crash is loud and unlike a normal death: the hull is thrown up, lands on its belly and throws a ring of dust, and it looks like a bunker from above.
The health bar changes to a fortification-style bar with a bunker icon, and the kill feed reports a crash, not a kill.
Teammates see the riders' icons and their reduced health above the shell.
Players inside get a warning when the shell is nearly gone, and a short countdown starts when the last of them leaves.
Hits from weapons that are good against fortifications show a stronger spark, so attackers learn what works.
changes_from_rts: In the source everyone still inside dies when the bunker falls. Under the game's proposal that players are thrown out of a dying vehicle hurt, they are thrown out hurt instead; losing several players at once to one kill is too heavy.

In the source the crash takes half of each rider's full health, so riders already down to half or less die in it (the wiki says instead that all survive at half health). Here it hurts every player inside but kills nobody, so no one dies to a blow aimed at the vehicle, while the loss stays large enough that the first kill still costs the team.
The source bus has no weapon of its own, so its driver would have nothing to do in the shell. Here the driver's seat becomes a firing port.
The source shell falls apart about a second after it is emptied. That is kept, with a short countdown, so an empty bunker is never left on the map for free.
In an RTS the second bar is bigger than the first. With players inside, a smaller bar is enough; the fresh bar is there to make a moment, not to double the vehicle.
The switch from a vehicle's armour to a fortification's is hidden in an RTS's armour tables. Here the bar style and hit sparks show it.
A driver with no riders gets only a short, weak last stand, because the shell is as strong as the players in it.

team_play.notes: The shell is worth what its riders are worth, and it shelters hurt teammates for as long as it stands. Engineers and medics have a reason to come to it, and the enemy has to coordinate a second kill with the right weapon.

notes: Needs the seat system with firing ports that passenger-sets-weapon's fire-ports twist already asks for.
The death flow has to branch: lethal damage is caught and turned into a change of state, with a new model, a static collision shape, a new health pool and a new armour set.
Every rider must stay seated through the change on all clients, and the driver's seat turns into a port.
A new static obstacle appears mid-match, so bot paths and vehicle paths around it must update, and it must be cleaned up when it falls or is emptied.
Kill credit and reward are split between the crash and the shell.
A fresh bar on a carrier with a full load of guns inside can become a fortress on the objective; a small bar, the fortification weaknesses and immobility keep it killable.
Dying on the point on purpose becomes a play. That is fine if the shell does not count for holding the point, or does so only briefly.
The health riders lose in the crash has to matter, or the first kill costs the carrier's team nothing.
If the crash pays nothing, attackers feel robbed; if both halves pay in full, the carrier feeds twice.
Players must see at once that the kill was not a kill: the crash and the new bar have to be unmistakable.
Who and how many are inside is hard to show from above.
The change of armour type is invisible without a bar style and an icon.

variants.name: Wreck fort
variants.summary: The lethal blow parks the carrier as a shell with fresh health; hurt riders stay in and fight from its ports until it is destroyed or emptied.

variants.name: Cover wreck
variants.summary: Everyone is thrown out hurt as on a normal death, but the dead hull stays behind as a piece of hard cover with its own health that players can fight around.
variants.seen_in: Our own reading for a player version, as written in passenger-sets-weapon's wreck-bunker twist; not in a source

adds_strengths.why: Even destroyed it leaves a piece of hard cover that its crew can fight around.

adds_weaknesses.why: The wreck is plain cover: it shelters nobody inside, and the enemy can use it too.

variants.name: Anchor by choice
variants.summary: The shell can also be entered on a key before the hull dies, one way; anchored, it gains room and lets riders fire who could not fire while it drove.

variants.name: Gun shell
variants.summary: A vehicle without passengers: the dead hull becomes a fixed gun post, and its own turret keeps working until the shell falls.
variants.seen_in: Our own idea for a one-player unit; not in a source

adds_strengths.why: Has to be destroyed twice: the first kill only parks it as a gun post with fresh health.

adds_weaknesses.why: Its second life can't move or turn its hull, so anything that outranges or flanks the gun post kills it at leisure.

variants.name: Booby-trapped shell
variants.summary: When the shell finally falls it explodes, hurting whoever came close to finish it.
variants.seen_in: Zero Hour Demolition General's Battle Bus, whose side-wide Demolitions upgrade adds a blast when it is finally destroyed (from the Battle Bus unit record)

variants.name: Timed rebirth
variants.summary: The shell is an egg: the unit can't act inside it, and if the shell survives a few seconds the unit comes back, whole or with the health the shell has left; it has a long cooldown.
variants.seen_in: Warcraft III Phoenix egg; League of Legends Anivia

adds_strengths.why: Comes back from a lethal blow if its shell survives a few seconds.

adds_weaknesses.why: Helpless in the shell, so enemies who keep shooting finish it, and the long cooldown means the next death is final.

countered_by.why: Enough burst left over after the kill breaks the helpless shell before its timer ends.

variants.name: Raise it again
variants.summary: If teammates repair the shell to full, the vehicle stands up and drives again.
variants.seen_in: Our own idea; no source does it (the Reckoner page says it can never pack up), and it pairs with recover-wreck

adds_strengths.why: Has to be destroyed twice: the first kill only parks it as a bunker with fresh health that its riders keep fighting from.

adds_weaknesses.why: Its second life can't move, so it stands wherever the hull happened to die, takes fortification-breaking weapons badly and holds hurt riders in one spot.

counters.why: Hit-and-run units can kill the hull, but lack the staying power or the heavy weapon to crack the shell that follows.

countered_by.why: The shell can't move, so artillery and fortification-breaking weapons level it from beyond its riders' reach.
Splash catches the hurt riders bunched together when the shell falls or when they climb out.

open_questions: Should the word lists also get a term for a second life (an on-death outcome or an armour model), so that a unit's on-death and armour fields can say it, or is the pattern enough? The Battle Bus carries fit notes asking for both; changing a word list is Mustafa's call.
When the shell falls, are the players inside thrown out hurt (recommended, in line with the on-death proposal) or killed, as in the source?
Does the driver stay inside with a firing port (recommended), or get thrown out at the crash to fight around the shell?
How is the kill reward split between the crash and the shell?
Does a shell on an objective count as holding it? (Recommended: no, or only for a short time.)

passenger-sets-weapon has a wreck-bunker twist that describes this mechanic as cover for players who were thrown out. Should that twist be retired and point here, with the cover-wreck twist in this file taking its place?

shooter_fit.reason: A loud, readable moment that turns a lost carrier into a last stand for several players at once, built on seats and firing ports the game needs anyway. It needs a clear second-bar read, a bounded shell and a rule for objectives.

review.notes: Sampled by the batch r3 checker (seed r3-2026-11-11), which covered 11 of the 33 batch patterns, and re-checked field by field against its sources; research/r3/checker/checks.json lists every field and verdict. Nothing was found wrong.
